utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As indicated yesterday by Judge Orie before we adjourned, he's not able to be with us today for urgent personal reasons, and Judge Fluegge and I have decided that it is in the interests of justice to carry on with the trial in his absence. In the absence of any preliminaries, can we call the witness. No preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have a short preliminary but I can do it while the witness is being brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So it's -- and good morning to you, I should say. It's just a housekeeping matter from yesterday, video 65 ter 22399a was MFI'd as P6923 pending provision of the CD to the Court Officer. That has now been done and therefore we would request that P6923 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any objections from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P6923 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number -- or it is already given an exhibit number. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Corokalo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would just like to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration that you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to pick off where we left off.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could please call up D785 in e-court and if we could turn to page 4 of that document. Once we get to page 4, I'll be asking that we focus on paragraph 15 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this paragraph, you talk of armed fights that took place in the Mahala neighbourhood. Can you tell me how those fights were initiated, how they came about?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The neighbourhood of Mahala is a broader area. It should be noted here that one part is called Muhici Mahala but it's all known as Mahala. By monitoring that area which is behind my house, near the Zdena river, it's on the right bank of Mahala, and on the left bank is my house and a number of Serb houses. So for our own security, we organised observation and monitoring to be prepared, and we noticed the people in the night hours, because this area is unlit. And even before these events, it was dangerous to go through this area because it's almost purely Muslim, 90 per cent Muslim. And in earlier days they were extreme, bent on fighting, et cetera. And since I had contact with them in football, it was a rare match that didn't end in a brawl. Anyway, we were observing that area, and in the night hours we noticed people who were going over there from our neighbourhood by night, and it was suspicious. And we noticed that people carrying hunting weapons were showing up there doing something, and then we organised ourselves and we realised something was going on there. Later, after the appeal was made to turn over those hunting rifles and other weapons that were registered with the police, they completely ignored it. Not only they but all the Muslims ignored it. And then an action was organised to collect these weapons, and in this effort there were incidents of shooting, skirmishes; not major fighting just skirmishes. So that was the reason for that conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You also mentioned two individuals here, Lola and Nail. Could you tell me please what the reputation these persons before the war.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I told you earlier that we had noticed that part of the non-Serb population from my street -- and at the end of my street there is a turn towards Otoci from which you could reach Mahala, which could be accessed also from another side, but I was interested in my street. Anyway, we noticed that some people from my area were going over there in the night hours. Nail and Lola did not have permanent residence there. Lola and Nail were the nicknames of people of whom I knew before the war. They passed through and sometimes stopped at my bar. Lola was in that area called Pobrijezje which was 5, 6 kilometres towards Sanski Most, and Nail lived in the centre of the town. Nail, in fact, is the name. And when we were gathering weapons, we found those people who were collecting weapons. I just ran into them because I didn't take part. We stayed over on our side of the river Zdena. Some people later told me that they found Nail and Lola in a house which was not theirs, in the house of a singer, they were sitting around, drinking whisky, smoking Marlboro cigarettes, and there were two guns on the table. So even before the war, these people were problematic. They would go to Italy, Germany, commit robberies, then they would be deported and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to look at paragraph 16, which is on the next page in both languages of your statement. And here you are talking about Hrustovo village and how it remained untouched until the time an elderly Muslim man killed Soldier Brajic with a rifle. Could you please tell us what do you mean by saying that it remained untouched until this time?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same story that happened in Mahala was going on in all the areas of Sanski Most, Hrustovo, Vrhpolje, everywhere. The drive to collect weapons that were requested was going on and what had been done until the afternoon went well. The population had not been provoked in any way. And when it was thought that it was all over, that we could relax, an incident occurred when a man, an elderly man, perhaps 70 or 80 years old, that's what Brajic, the chief with whom I later worked, told me, was killed by the brother of that Captain Brajic, and the conflict escalated after that killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you clarify for us. The transcript and the translation record that: The elderly man of 70 to 80 was killed by the brother of Captain Brajic. Is that what happened or something else?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The elderly Muslim man killed the brother of Captain Brajic, who was the commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I have, later there occurred an incident where some people ran out of control. We heard that there were casualties; I don't know how many. I wasn't there. That's the information I got from Veljko Brajic because they were cousins.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to look at paragraph 19, which is on the same page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you talk about Arkan's men. I would like for you to tell the Court how you first came to find out that Arkan's men were in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These events happened between the 16th and the 19th September 1995. According to a decision of the Crisis Staff, I was sent to the Kljuc front line with about 380 men that had been gathered. We called it the Worker's Battalion, all the people we could rally; teachers, even retired people, everybody was recruited. And although we were against using such people as the last defence of Sanski Most, we were sent towards Krupa - that is, from Benakovac to Turska Jasenica to Jasenica. We set out around 1600 hours. We got to Jasenica. Some people didn't even have weapons. Rapid action forces joined us on the road, and we managed as best we could. After a few days we had to retreat, and it was around Benakovac. So from the 16th to the 19th in those operations where we had 380 men, I was a security officer, we lost a couple of dozen men. We were not well armed enough. When I got back on the 19th in the evening, my wife told me that Arkan's men had arrived at the hotel. The hotel was well lit. The men were given food, as normal in a hotel. On the 20th when we got to Privredna Banka, which were our place to report, I found Arkan's men there. They were controlling all vital facilities. The man was not saying a word, and we had difficulty reaching the command because he had captured some people, tied them to trees, shaved their heads, et cetera. Anyway, they had come somehow between the 18th and the 19th. On whose orders, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Those people -- those people that were -- those people that were tied to trees and with their heads shaven, did you know who they were?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them. I didn't have the chance because I wasn't there physically. But later during that month that we stayed there, we found the hotel manager, whose head was shaved. I asked him how it happened, and he explained that one of Arkan's commanders who got angry because they had to go somewhere on duty, do a stint, and come back by bus in the evening, and they would get angry because their meals were not hot, the food was not ready, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get some clarification --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- here. Mr. Corokalo, if you look at page 6, starting from line 19, you're telling us about the 20th when people -- when you got Privredna Banka, and you say you found Arkan's men there. They were controlling all vital facilities. Then you said: "The man was not saying a word, and we had difficulty reaching the command because he had captured some people." Which man is this? Who is this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The man who was the security guard outside that building. We had our command in that bank. It was a man of Arkan's who was outside the bank with whom we were in contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were responsible for security in your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, how would you describe the attitude of the brigade as to or towards Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say for sure because during that month before I fled Sanski Most, I was unable to find out how they had arrived, at whose invitation. I know that my entire section of the brigade was engaged in the Sanski Most-Kljuc front. None of us were there. Between the 16th and the 19th, there were some police officers left in town. But since all the men from the brigade were in position and he was in the hotel, I couldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But how was the interaction between you and then Arkan's men on the 20th when you met them at Privredna Banka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had a major problem explaining that we had just come back the previous night, that our forces were crushed, that we had no idea where most of our men were. But they were arrogant and we gave them a wide berth. We feared them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did they shave your heads like they had done to the other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We kept telling them that we had just arrived that night and that we were supposed to see the commander to see what we were going to do, how to find our men, and it was difficult to convince them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you speak here of Muslims and Croats, 1.000 inhabitants in various neighbourhoods that were -- that were mis -- that had harm done to them by these Arkan's forces. First I want to ask you: The territory that these Croats and Muslims lived upon, was it controlled by the VRS or by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time we had the whole town under our control, but those people had just decided to stay. The entire neighbourhood known as Aganovici on the right bank of the Sana River, which means from the hotel and the municipality building, up to the part called Poljaci, populated mainly by Croats. So there were about a thousand Muslims and Croats who just stayed, to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And had those Muslims and Croats that stayed there caused any trouble or fought against the VRS during the prior four years?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I know some of those people personally. One of them played football with me. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you say that Arkan -- that all harm was done to them by Arkan and his men. What do you mean by that, if you have any details?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a chance to get any information about that because I didn't spend any of that time in town. The whole period until I left Sanski Most, I was near the Novsko front line. I was touring our units to tell men that some of our people were missing, and if somebody shows up they shouldn't shoot. They should treat them carefully. We had lost 98 men. I know that four or five had got out, a few were found and identified. For the rest, I don't know to this day where they ended up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, on behalf of General Mladic and the rest of my team, I thank you for answering my questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Jeremy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question to the witness before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- the floor is for the Prosecution. Mr. Corokalo, I would like to clarify one matter. It's me speaking at the moment. You described where and under which circumstances you met the two men with the two men with the nicknames Lola and Nail in a private house drinking whisky and smoking cigarettes. In your statement, you told us they were known as commanders of paramilitary units. You didn't mention that in your answers to Mr. Ivetic. Could you explain that a little bit more, what kind of units and what is the basis of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that I saw those men. When the operation ended, I inquired from my men - I had to for security reasons - and they told me they had found those men in that house. We knew they didn't live there. What were they doing there if they weren't part of some organisation? Those were our conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this clarification that you personally didn't meet them in the house. Second, you say in paragraph 15 - perhaps we can get that back on the screen; it's the previous page - they were known as commanders of paramilitary units. Not as members but commanders. That is in your statement. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, the word "komandir" or "leader," that's questionable. From our information, these men had contacts in Italy, in Germany. We knew that they were of suspicious background. We knew they had been involved in smuggling before and they had been deported. And then by inquiring, we found out that these men had a say in these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In which things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Arming, distribution of weapons to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is your understanding of the term "commander"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a follow-up. But even doing what you say they did does not necessarily make them members of any paramilitary unit. They could have just been armed traffickers. What makes you think that they belonged to a paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the conclusion as to whether they were members of paramilitary units or were just helping in the arming, for me that's one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see. So you actually have no basis for concluding that they belonged to a paramilitary unit except for thinking that: If you arm people, therefore you do belong to a paramilitary unit. That's the only basis? Thank you so much. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Corokalo.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now I'd like to begin by just taking a few minutes to clarify where you were and when during the war period. So in paragraph 4 of your statement, we read that in September 1991 you were deployed to the Jasenovac theater; and later, in 1992, you returned to Lusci Palanka, Sanski Most. Now, this return was in early April 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And were you also in Sanski Most in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's possible that I was there. I could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So you -- you returned a month before the return of your units in April. You came become in a personal capacity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the unit returned to Lusci Palanka, we went around, liaison officers, as it were, some of us, who kept contact with the population in Sanski Most. We would go back to Sanski Most to keep in touch, so we didn't have to be there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But according to your recollection, you returned back to Sanski Most for a period of [sic] March 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. At about that time. Sometime in the spring, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 4, we read that on your return to Sanski Most, which I read as the return of your unit, you were sent home where you stayed until May 1992. Now, when in May 1992 did you return to active duty?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't returned to active duty in the brigade immediately. We remained as liaison officers, a certain number of men, we remained there to work with the TO with some of our men who were trying to self-organise, to establish local parts of the town, to organise them. And because I was involved in sports and all these activities before the war, we felt that this was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last portion of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, could you -- we only heard a part of your answer. So we heard that you were "involved in sports and all these activities before the war, we felt that this was ..." and then we didn't hear the end of your answer. Could you repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We decided that I and several other men who were men of significance because we were involved with sports and those activities, we decided that we should return to the town and organise people and return people to activities that were ongoing then and that were the result of all the developments there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this period during which you were working as a liaison officer with the -- working with the TO, was that in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this went on for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. Now you became -- we read in your statement that you were a -- that you were a security officer at the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, your superior was Reserve Captain First Class Pero Milicevic, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And his superior in the 1st Krajina Corps, the chief of the organ for intel and security in May and June, was Colonel Milan Stevilovic, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that part. Pero was in charge of us, the reservists, but I didn't know about the chain of command going upwards. I wasn't in a position to know at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. And if I tell you that Colonel Stevilovic was replaced by Colonel Stevan Bogajevic in early 1992, do you know about that or is that also up the chain of command to a level that you're not aware of?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement and during your testimony yesterday and today, you talked about questioning persons from Hrustovo and Vrhpolje. Now, this questioning was carried out during early June 1992, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those were the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes. And was this questioning carried out in early June 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you. This was sometime in May or June, but I can't really be specific about this period. There were a lot of developments, but I know that that period was approximately the way you put it, but I can't recall every detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you carried out this questioning in your capacity as a security officer in the brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, we'll come back to those events, but for now I want to continue with the chronology of your war history. Now, at various points in your statement, you discussed your involvement in Operation Corridor, including at Modrica, Odzak, and Gradac. Now, it's not always clear to me when you're referring to the involvement of your brigade in these operations and when you're referring to your own personal involvement so that's something that I want to clarify. Now, you say that you went along with the 3rd Battalion to Operation Corridor where you relieved the 1st Battalion of your brigade. Now, that 1st Battalion was also known as the Crni Djordje Battalion; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not correct. I didn't say that I was with the 1st Battalion. I was with the 3rd. The 1st Battalion preceded us. We relieved them. So I came to relieve the 1st Battalion in early June. The corridor was breached on the 28th of June. So I came as a relief for the 1st Battalion. It was never called the 1st Battalion. It was never called the Crni Djordje. The 1st was called the 1st, the 2nd was called the 2nd, and the 3rd was the 3rd. And me, as a member of the 3rd Battalion, I came to relieve the 1st Battalion. And then later we went to Modrica and Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. The 1st Battalion, was that commanded by Captain Milovan Lazic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Miroslav Radakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you a document in connection with these answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could we please see P2419. And this is a report from the command of the 6th Partizan Brigade, and specifically the 10th Partizan Battalion to the 6th Partizan Brigade forward command post. And it's dated the 15th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you take a look at the document on the left side of your screen, in the first paragraph we read that: "Based on the Order of the 6th Partizan Brigade Command," and we see the strictly confidential number, "of the 13th of July, 1992, the 10th Partizan Battalion Command has replaced the Crni Djordje Battalion" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "Replenished."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Excuse me, "replenished the Crni Djordje battalion with the following VO," which earlier in the document we read is an abbreviation for military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, could we please go to page 4 in the English and 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, we see a list of 94 names, and number 92 is Dusko Corokalo, security officer. That's you; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, this -- this order is dated the 15th of July, 1992. This is the order that pursuant to which you were first sent to the corridor operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- well, actually, I've never seen this order before. I wasn't with the 1st Battalion. I relieved them. Perhaps it was planned for me to be there, but I never received this kind of order. What happened was Pero Malicevic came. It was probably planned that I should be with the 1st Battalion for I don't know what reasons, and I actually went there as a replacement of the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go back to the first page, please, of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, the way that I read this list is that the -- the list of names are those persons who are replenishing or, to put it another way, replacing the Crni Djordje Battalion. And, therefore, on that basis, my reading of this document is that, pursuant to this order, you -- you were sent to the corridor as a replacement for persons in the Crni Djordje Battalion.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I state with full responsibility that this is the first time that I ever have seen this document. I never had it in my hands, and I see that it was signed by Milovan Lazic. Now, whether there was a plan for me to be there, I really don't know anything about that. But what I do know is that the 1st Battalion of the 6th Sana Brigade was never referred to as Crni Djordje. There was a group from Palanka that was called Crni Djordje. As for the 1st Battalion, as I said, this is the first time that I lay my eyes on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. And it's -- I understand that you haven't seen the document before and that's -- that's not important. My purpose of showing you this document was an attempt to date the time that you went to the corridor operation. Now, you've said that you were involved in operations in Sanski Most in early June 1992. So can you give us a date when you were first sent from Sanski Most to the corridor operation?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Battalion was already at the corridor, and I went there as a replacement. Now, the -- on the 28th of June, the corridor was broken through, so I was there in -- at the beginnings. I can't recall the date, but I was there when it was broken through, and I remained there till mid-August; some 40 days or so. About 40 days, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So you were there from -- so you left in mid-August and you arrived 40 days before that. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. In mid-August, I had already returned to Sanski Most but with the 3rd Battalion. The commander was Ranko or Branko Predojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now after you returned to Sanski Most, I understand you were there for a period of time before being sent to Gradacac. How long were you in Sanski Most from mid-August?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I returned from the corridor, some 10 to 15 days at most, I was off duty. We called it a rest period. Because there weren't many of us security officers, we couldn't spend a lot time resting. So I was then re-engaged as needed. So it couldn't have been more than 15 days, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. So can we agree that you were in Sanski Most from early April to late June/early July, at which point you were sent to the corridor operation. You then returned in mid-August and you remained in Sanski Most for 10 to 15 days. And then, after that, I understand you were -- you left Sanski Most and you were in other war theatres and you didn't return until 1995, the autumn of 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to move on, and I'd like to discuss the Mahala which you mention in your statement and which you have discussed with Mr. Ivetic this morning. Now, when you refer to Mahala in paragraph 17 of your statement, you're referring to events on the 25th of May, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really tell you with certainty about the date, whether it's exact, but all the events happened at that time, approximately. All the events in that territory. But I would also just like to tell you that Mahala is just a neighbourhood. It starts near my house on the right-hand side. The problem was with Otoke, as far as the defence of my part of the town was concerned. So the neighbourhood Otoke on the right hand of the Sana River, Otoke, Muhici, and Mahala. So it wasn't just Mahala. It was these neighbourhoods, the three: Mahala, Otoke, and Muhici. Now my house was on the left-hand side, on the left bank of the Sana, and we were, in fact, on the forward lines of the front line, the line of separation with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, were you actually personally involved in what you described as the -- in your -- in paragraph 17 of your statement as the "armed fights" in Mahala, or were you at the command post in Lusci Palanka at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was in Sanski Most as I've already said. I was in my cafe bar. We self-organised, as I already mentioned. We had some kind of staff there of ours. I was there. Now, the unit that was then brought by Radak, that was the first time I saw that man, I believe he was a captain. Now, I was responsible to show them the line where it begins towards Otoke, Mahala, and Muhici. They are all one whole. So I actually introduced them to the area. I led them to the area because my house was right there. So then I had to go back home to my home because we didn't know how the whole thing was going further to develop.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And how close is your cafe bar to Mahala?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from Otoke, that's where it was connected. But from Mahala, it was about 2 kilometres further up. But from Otoke itself, it was about 200 metres. That's where my house was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, were you -- were you among the Serb forces that entered Mahala on the 25th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only at the beginning, at the Otoke end. So you have to bear that in mind. I was there at the Otoke end. I led the units there. I didn't go through Muhic or Mahala, I was just the intro for Radak into Otoke and then I went back to my position, to my house, my coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 15 of your statement, you refer to Serb forces finding a large quantity of automatic weapons and a 60-millimetre mortar in Mahala. Now, this morning you've testified that you noticed people carrying hunting weapons at night going from your area in the direction of Mahala. Were you involved in counting the weapons found by Serb forces in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, definitely not. But I was telling you about the beginning. At the start people with hunting weapons were seen, but I couldn't go in depth. That was not allowed. You couldn't get to Mahala or Otoke. Even before the war it wasn't easy to walk there at night safely. Now, this part and -- including Mahala, where there were a lot of people of Muslim ethnicity, about 90 per cent of the people there were Muslim, they were of low levels of education. They were problematic people. They would cause trouble. And you would have a problem if you decided to go there, because these people were as they were, they would start brawls and street fights and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So I think you -- you answered my question in the first sentence of your answer with, "no, no, definitely not." So you weren't involved in counting of the weapons collected in Mahala. Now in paragraph 15, you say that Serb forces found a large quantity of automatic weapons and a 60-millimetre mortar. Now, what is the basis of your knowledge for this claim in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I got that bit of information from the men who had been there. We were interested to learn what had happened there, so I was told by these men when they returned that they had found weapons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Were these men members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Automatic weapons, interpreter's addition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the 6th Sana Brigade, yes. But the members -- my unit of the Territorial Defence did not. This part of the street. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did they give you an indication of the number of automatic weapons that they had found?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one mentioned in that sense the number of weapons. But, as I said, there was a large quantity or largish quantity of weapons, including that 60-millimetre mortar. But the exact number, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So no one mentioned a number to you but you, nevertheless, believed that there was a large quantity of weapons there -- found there?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "large," that term, in this general story, yes. We -- the information from the people we learned -- we learned from the people who were returning was that there was a large quantity, but what exactly the number was I really wouldn't know. But that was the term they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to put it to you that the reality is that there wasn't a large quantity of weapons found in Mahala. In fact, no significant amounts of weapons were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object. Your Honours, can we have a bases for this then?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P2889.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, coming up on our screens is a report from the SJB chief Mirko Vrucinic to the Banja Luka security services centre, and -- so it's from the Banja Luka security services centre, and it's dated the 15th of June, 1992. And, sir, did you -- so you knew who Mirko Vrucinic was at this time, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no Marko Vrucinic but there was Mirko Vrucinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 3 of this document, we read: "On the 25th of May 1992, this 'disarming' was followed by a military action (attack) against the downtown neighbourhood of Mahala, which resulted in the capture of 2.000 civilians but no significant amounts of weapons have been found because they had been concealed earlier." And, sir, that's the reality, isn't it, that no significant amounts of weapons were found?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for context I would ask that the next paragraph be also presented which provides more information about "the Muslim population had been relatively well armed predominantly with infantry weapons, mines, and explosives."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess you can do that in re-examination, Mr. Ivetic. Carry on, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And I would just like the witness to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Which is that the reality is that no significance -- no significant amounts of weapons were found in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you. You are contesting the -- in the sense that you are denying the information that I received. Now what is a significant quantity, I -- you know, it's hard to determine, but this was done in a report by the police, and that's different. Now, if you ask the men who had actually been there and they tell you, then that's a different issue. Now it's a difference in terminology. They use this term there in this report, but whether a significant quantity is five or ten or -- what that means to an ordinary man, that's a debatable issue, but weapons were there. There were weapons found according to this document that I see before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll leave that there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I know we are at break time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We take a break. Before we do so, sir, may you please -- we're going to take a break for 20 minutes and please get back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We take a break and come back at 5 to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness may be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to resume by discussing events in Hrustovo and Vrhpolje in late May, early June 1992. So in your statement in paragraph 17, you state that: "After the armed fights in Mahala, I went to the Gradacac war theater and I stayed there until the end of the war." Now, from the -- the questions and answers today, I think that this is correct, that we've established that you actually went to the corridor in late June, early July; therefore, not immediately after the events in Mahala. And therefore, I'd like to ask you about these events that happened in Hrustovo and Vrhpolje in early June period. Now, were you personally involved in the disarming operations in Hrustovo and Vrhpolje in late May, early June 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. And in -- so in paragraph 16, and I think you've mentioned this also today, when you -- when you say that you emphasize that the Hrustovo village remained untouched until an elderly Muslim man killed Soldier Brajic with a rifle, that's something that you heard from others; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, even though you were not involved in the disarming operations, you were nevertheless involved in questioning persons captured during those operations; that's correct, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean that you are not putting certain things right. What happened in Hrustovo with the killing of Brajic's brother has nothing to do with the action I took later, when that group from Golaja was exchanged. Then we went through a process of screening, looking for people who were aiders and abettors, people we had information about. One action was the murder of Brajic's brother, and one other action - a completely different action - was when we were screening people looking for helpers. We had operative information and we wanted to identify people who were helpers to those from Golaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So do I understand it correctly that you were -- you were not involved in questioning persons captured during the late May, early June disarming operations in Vrhpolje and Hrustovo. Instead, you were involved in questioning persons captured in Golaja woods; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, the action of capturing people when Brajic's brother was killed, I didn't participate, but later in Golaja I participated in the screening operation, looking for helpers. I was not present when Brajic's brother was killed and I did not take part in that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But my question is whether you asked questions of persons captured during the disarming operations in Hrustovo and Vrhpolje in late May and early June.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was part of that operation, but you have to separate the killing of that Brajic from that operation. The two have nothing in common.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now while you were questioning these persons captured during the disarming operations in Hrustovo and Vrhpolje, I'd like to ask you about what information you were able to obtain, and I'd like to ask you about two particular incidents. Now, this Trial Chamber has received evidence that on the 31st of May, 1992 Serb soldiers killed 27 unarmed civilians who were sheltering in a garage in Hrustovo. During your interview of persons from this area, did you learn any information about this particular event?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard anything about the killing of people in a garage. I was not in charge of operative work on the ground. We had a classroom in a school house, and we were looking for certain people. I remember one nickname, Zeka, we were looking for him. Unfortunately, we didn't find him. I didn't leave that room for two days and one night. I never heard about the killing of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, did you subsequently hear about this event or you'd never heard about it before?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Never heard. Because the people who did the operative work, I don't even know them. Because the geographic area of Hrustovo and Vrhpolje is very large. I didn't even have a chance to meet them. I don't know the area at all except for the Hrustovo cave, where I went on a school trip as a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But you were questioning persons captured in this area during late May, early June, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Brajo Grman [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, the second instant I was to ask you about was an event on Vrhpolje bridge also on the 31st of May, 1992. Now, this Trial Chamber has received evidence that their soldiers rounded up the inhabitants of Begejci near Vrhpolje, took the men to Vrhpolje bridge, beat them, forced them to jump off, and shot them with automatic weapons as they did. Did you learn about this incident during your interview of captured persons from Vrhpolje?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That incident again is not related to what I was doing, but I know about that incident. I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did you hear about it during the interviews that you were carrying out?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I returned to town, I heard about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So you heard about it contemporaneously? You heard about it in early June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right after, during those few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did you learn that the perpetrators of this incident were members of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know from which units they were. This did not leak to the public, but people were talking around town and I checked it. But as to what units were involved, I did not inquire.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 13 of your statement, we read that the interviews that you were involved in were conducted at the elementary school in Vrhpolje, and you've mentioned that a few times during your direct testimony. What was the name of that school, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Look, the Vrhpolje area is large, unfamiliar to me. There was one old school and one new school. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in that same paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, have you been in the old school or in the new school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The old one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, in that same paragraph 13, you emphasize that the individuals that you spoke to were not detained either during or after the interview. Now, during your testimony yesterday at transcript page 28430, lines 10 to 14, referring to your screening of individuals at this school, you said, and I quote: "I participated in the screening or the questioning of people because the logistics wanted to have certain number of people. I and another two co-workers of mine worked on that. We never left the room and therefore I don't know what happened to them afterwards, where they went and so on." So just to clarify, which of those two accounts is correct? Do you know that the individuals you spoke to were not detained after the interview, or do you not know about what happened to them after the interview?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have that information. I didn't get a chance to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. Now leaving aside those persons that you interviewed who you don't know whether or not they were detained, you nevertheless know that other individuals captured during the operations in Mahala, Vrhpolje, and Hrustovo were detained in various locations in Sanski Most, including the sports hall, Betonirka, and later the Krings factory hall. You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And were you also personally present at those facilities between May and July 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never was at Betonirka. I was present by the sports hall because it's close to my house. The sports hall is near the bank of the Zdena river. And I was at Krings as well because I had heard that some elderly people were being held there because in the Second World War they had displayed solidarity. I just went to check that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you're also aware that many persons held at the locations that I've mentioned and that you've also added to were taken to Manjaca camp, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the Manjaca camp when that operation began. The news spread around town. But, of course, I didn't know in advance whom they would be taking way. We couldn't learn that from our sources. When I heard that it was happening, and it was about 500 metres from my coffee bar where we had our headquarters, I went there to see what's going on. I spent about an hour there but only as an observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, just to clarify, when you say "I heard that it was happening," here you're referring to the transport of captured persons to Manjaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you -- you seem to be referring to a particular incident. Do you refer to the -- do you recall the date of that, date of that transportation?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't remember dates because all these things happened in a short period. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And were you involved in securing this particular convoy? Were colleagues of yours involved in securing this particular convoy?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. And none of my colleagues from my street participated either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: How about the colleagues who weren't from your street? Did you recognise any persons who were involved in securing the convoys?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I was standing near the main entrance and they were on the flank of the sports hall. We were not allowed to go around. You could not go anywhere close to them. We were standing on the plateau outside the secondary school centre. It was a couple of hundred metres away that we were standing. There were lots of people around.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move to another topic, I have a question to one point. You told us about your questioning of people in the school. Mr. Jeremy quoted from the transcript of yesterday, and there I read: "I participated in the screening of the questioning of people because the logistics wanted to have certain number of people." Who is "the logistics"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The men from our Crisis Staff, our defence. We had a certain list of names that we were looking for. I remember one nickname, Zeka. Of course, there were more people on the list that we were supposed to find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what does it mean: "They wanted to have certain number of people"? Just a number of people or what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had a list of names, a certain number of names of people whom we were supposed to find to determine whether they were still in the area or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But I understood your testimony that you were responsible for questioning the people. They were brought to you. How can you work on finding people if you're not out in the field in the town or wherever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The three of us, we had a list of people. The people who did the operative work on the ground were looking and bringing people to us, and then we would look on -- at the list and see if the person was on the list or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And for that purpose, just to identify them, they were brought to the school where you were working together with two co-workers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have another question. A little bit earlier you were asked about the incident at the Vrhpolje bridge, and you said you heard about this event during those few days. You say you heard that "by people talking around town and I checked it." I really don't understand. Can you explain that a little bit further. From whom did you hear that and what did you check?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The events that I mentioned in those few days, all of this transpired in a couple of days, Golaja, Mahala, these were linked events, and of course I wasn't always present in all those locations. Now, I heard of these things when I returned to the town, and then I would hear about an incident. There were a number of people that I trusted, and then when I got information from them, whether something had actually happened or not and what had transpired, I would -- I received the information from those men and confirmed that that had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you knew these men from before, these people from whom you received this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. These were people from Territorial Defence who worked with me on gathering intelligence. They were credible people. They weren't people who would spread rumours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you give me the names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't specifically mention any names for any specific events because these -- all these events were linked and I couldn't really remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said you knew these people from before and you trusted them, and now you say you don't know who it was who told you about this specific event at the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I knew those people, all those people, all of us who were there together who worked with me. I trusted them and I received some information -- this information from them. We received information, approximately all of us, we would receive the same type of information in those couple of days. Now, I cannot remember as I sit here specifically who told me about this particular event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, just before we -- we move away from this issue of the transportation of persons from the sports hall to Manjaca, you've said that you and those persons on your street were not involved in securing that particular convoy. It's correct, though, that other members of the VRS provided security for that convoy, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move to another topic, the departure of non-Serbs from Sanski Most. Now, in paragraph 19 of your statement, you say that: "Until the arrival of Arkan in 1995, there were several neighbourhoods with more than a thousand inhabitants of Muslim and Croat ethnicities in Sanski Most." Now, you've said today that Arkan arrived in Sanski Most in September 1995, yes? Now -- so -- I see that you're shaking your head, if you could just verbalise a response, just "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 16th, I left and he wasn't this. He appeared sometime between the 16th and the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you -- you're aware that before Arkan arrived in the period between 1991 and February 1995, tens of thousands of Muslims and Croats, numbering the overwhelming majority of these ethnic groups, had left Sanski Most; you are aware of that, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the security organ in your brigade was also aware that during 1992 Muslim and Croat populations were -- were moving out of Sanski Most on a massive scale, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now in connection with this answer, I'd like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31603.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, coming up now on the screen before you is a report dated the 3rd of August, 1992 to the Prijedor operations and tactical group security chief, and it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we go down to the bottom of the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We see that it's from the security chief, Captain First Class Pero Malicevic. He was your boss, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to focus on paragraph 1 of this document, a "Situation in the Territory," and we read: "Constant control of the territory in the brigade's area of responsibility has been established. There isn't any new intelligence about the enemy's activities. The Muslim and Croatian populations are moving out on a massive scale. This, in our opinion, should be done selectively, in accordance with set criteria. There is a potential threat coming from those who are combat ready and likely to join the enemy's ranks." Sir, you're aware that in August 1992 the civilian and military organs of Sanski Most launched an initiative whereby Muslims and Croats who wanted to stay in Sanski Most were required to make a written request to stay and to provide a declaration of loyalty. You're aware of that, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this was the procedure that was followed -- that had been followed by those Muslims and Croats who were still in Sanski Most in the autumn of 1995 when Arkan was present, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that's how it was. I don't really know for certain. I had a colleague who worked at the bank and who, until the very end almost, was with me and he played football with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just to clarify your answer, that was a Muslim colleague, I take it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He, Rufad, these were the men who remained until very late. Now whether they had signed loyalty, I never asked because it wouldn't do. Probably they did something in keeping with the law because -- and that's how they acted, but -- and -- but they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31603 receives number P6924, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to finish today by discussing your evidence in relation to Arkan, which you refer to in paragraph 19 of your statement and you've mentioned him a few times today. Now, referring to those Muslims and Croats in Sanski Most in 1995, in paragraph 19 of your statement, you say that all the harm that was done to those Muslims and Croats was done by Arkan and his men. Now, here you're referring to the arresting and abusing of non-Serbs in Sanski Most by Arkan and his men, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct you. You said 1991 but this was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. If that's what I said, that was my mistake. I mean 1995. But just to ask you to answer my question, this -- this arresting and abusing of non-Serbs is what Arkan was doing in Sanski Most in 1995, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Because those men who were there, there was no reason whatsoever. I mean, had we wanted to do anything, we could have done it a long time ago. But when they arrived there, Arkan's men, then they handled these people. And I was busy at the time, but I know that there were some ten or so people that I knew that I didn't see there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you a document in connection with this, with Arkan's presence in Sanski Most in September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P3095.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, this -- this document is a dispatch from the RS MUP forwarding to the deputy minister and the public security department a proposal of General Mladic to the RS MUP and the president of the Republika Srpska. And it's dated the 23rd of September, 1995. I'd like to look at that actual proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Which is on the second page of this document in each language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So we see that this letter is dated the 23rd of September, 1995, and we see it is to the president of RS and the RS Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we could just go to page 3, please, in each language, just to see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see it's type-signed by Colonel General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go back to page 2, please. Thank you, Mr. Usher. And so page 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, we read in the first sentence that the formations of the SDG, Serbian Volunteer Guard, known as Tigrovi, under the command of Zeljko Raznjatovic, aka Arkan, are in the zone of the 1st Battalion of the 1st Brigade of the 2 KK. Now, in the second paragraph, we see details about what Arkan has been doing. We read that he's being bullying VRS officers, and at the end of the first sentence in the second paragraph, halfway down, we see that he's been arresting and abusing non-Serbs. Now if we go to the fourth paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we'll need to go to the next page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We read that: "The presence of Arkan's paramilitary units precipitated armed clashes and incidents with individuals and some VRS units, and upset the population at large after word got out that he arrested all the Muslims in Sanski Most and liquidated a certain number of loyal Muslim citizens, including family members of some VRS servicemen, justifying it publicly as liquidation of an infiltrated sabotage group in Grdanovci village." Sir, this is the sort of behaviour that you made reference to in your statement and during your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for this one part, that's how it was. This was about the men that I knew were there and this would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, at the end of the paragraph that we've just been looking at, we see that General Mladic makes some requests and proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in the English, please. Sorry, actually could we go back one -- one page in the English. But just go to the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So we see that the first request is that: "The President of the RS should revoke his decision that gave Zeljko Raznjatovic the power to make arrests, mistreat, disarm and take away VRS members and civilians ..." Now, sir, were you aware that Arkan was making these arrests and mistreating civilians in Sanski Most pursuant to a decision by President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And before we leave this document, sir, I'd just like to focus on the final point, 4, where we read: "If the competent state organs who engaged Zeljko Raznjatovic to carry out unlawful activities fail to take steps within their jurisdiction, then VRS units shall carry out the order of the President of RS on disarming paramilitary organisations that are not under the specific command of the VRS GS." Now, sir, in the week that followed the writing of this letter, General Mladic's military notebook --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that's P364, pages 72 to -3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- indicates that he first met with President Karadzic and discussed Arkan, and then a day later, he met the chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav army, Momcilo Perisic, and the head of the Serbian state security, Jovica Stanisic, and again discussed Arkan and specifically his presence in Sanski Most. Now, were you aware of these meetings through your role in the security organ or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge of this meeting, and I didn't have any occasion to know. Because in my post it wasn't possible for me to obtain this information, this type of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we won't dwell on those entries. Now, following the conduct of Arkan and his men in Sanski Most, as described by you and by General Mladic in this letter to Radovan Karadzic that we've just looked at, rather than arrest Arkan or kick him out of the VRS's area of responsibility, the VRS started co-ordinating with Arkan in Prijedor. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. And I couldn't know this. And secondly, the operations where I was at the Novsko theater, I was there with my men and couldn't know this or was this possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P3094 on our screens. And, Your Honours, as this document is being brought up, I'll mention that a revised translation of P3094 has been uploaded into e-court under doc ID P0046440/A/ET. And as we'll see when we look at the document, it is a -- the English translation of Milovanovic is -- currently reads as "Milanovic," and so we would request that the revised translation replace the one currently in e-court. And obviously Mr. Ivetic will take a look at that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is an order dated the 11th of October, 1995. It's from the RS MUP Minister Tomislav Kovac to the chief of the Prijedor CJB. We see that it is copied to, among others, the VRS General Staff. Now, below this list of persons the document was sent to, we read: "Pursuant to the agreement between the MUP Minister and the Chief of the VRS GS, Manojlo Milovanovic," in the B/C/S, "I hereby order ..." And we see that the order requires the chief of the Prijedor CJB, Zeljko Raznjatovic, and the commander of the Janja Detachment, to start arresting deserters in Prijedor. And in the final sentence we read that: "This task should be carried out together with unit commands if they are in the area, and if they are not, further command should be agreed with the main staff." Now, sir, following the co-ordination described in this document, were you aware that Arkan would go on to commit the same crimes in Prijedor that he'd just committed in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Can we have a basis for how the witness would know about this? He's asking him to speculate. If the witness has said, previously at page 40, line 9, that he couldn't know anything about this from 9 to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has talked extensively about Arkan. Mr. Ivetic spent five or so transcript pages discussing Arkan with the witness. The witness is in this area at the time, and I would suggest it's a perfectly reasonable question for me to ask him if he is aware of what Arkan was doing in Prijedor during the exact same time-period the witness has already discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Object overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Put, Your Honours, the witness has already said he doesn't know. So how can he ask him again now were you aware?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He can tell us if he knows or doesn't know about this one. He didn't know what happened earlier. Now it's about something different, and if he doesn't know, he can tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, I'll repeat my question about whether you were aware that Arkan would go on to commit the same crimes in Prijedor that he had just committed in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO COROKALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't possibly have known that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now to finish my questions and to finish this chapter, I'd like to show you a document where these events were reported in the press, and I'll ask you if you had an opportunity to see those in the press even though you may not have been in Prijedor at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please see 65 ter 31619.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, on the screen before you is an article that appeared in the Serbian publication Vreme International on the 16th of October, 1995. So that's five days after the order that we just looked at. The dead-line is -- sorry, the head line is a "A job fit for the Tigers." Now, in the first sentence of the first paragraph, we read that: "According to field reports, after the launch of the offensive on Western Bosnia, Arkan's men mounted earlier last month a huge campaign of enforcing order in a manner" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the left part of the -- the first paragraph on the left column be enlarged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I read on: "... in a manner already seen in Eastern Slavonia: By forcibly recruiting people, shaving their heads, and beating them (if necessary)." And I'll skip to the third paragraph and the sentence beginning with the word "nevertheless." "Nevertheless, the Tigers have undoubtedly encountered resistance from the VRS." And I'd like now to look at the last paragraph of -- sorry, the last sentence of paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could just go down a little bit in the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in the last sentence of paragraph 2, we read that: "General Mladic quickly recognised the danger and, in a recent interview, commented on 'groups and paramilitaries who gather mostly around goldsmiths' and banks but have never liberated one little hill.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now continuing on, we read: "Nevertheless, it seems that for now Zeljko Raznjatovic works more for the benefit than to the detriment of the Republika Srpska authorities. One of the reasons why the misunderstandings have been so quickly ironed out might be the unequivocal success of the operation launch in late September in which the area around Prijedor was cleansed of Muslims and Croats. According to UNHCR reports, members of the Serbian ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could we go down in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "... members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard expelled about 5.000 people to the territory under the control ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should have that part in B/C/S on the screen. I don't know where it is on that page, but on the right side or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, I did see that. But the end of the sentence is not visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yeah, could we go across and up, please. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Continuing on. I'll read the sentence again. "According to UNHCR reports, members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard expelled about 5.000 people to the territory under the control of the BH Government within only a few days. Kris Janowsky, the UNHCR porte-parole in Sarajevo, says that this was done in 'a rather ghastly way.' According to the same reports, worn-out people were forced to swim across the river and many drowned during the attempt. Others died of exhaustion and beatings. All them were thoroughly looted. The testimonies are by women, children and the elderly men: The men were made to board the buses with Vukovar licence plates and were taken to an unknown location." Sir, would you agree that, according to this report, Arkan and his men continued in Prijedor what they had started in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Again, he's asking the same question that the witness now has two times said he doesn't know what was going on in Sanski -- pardon me, in Prijedor at that time. So, again, if we're getting to reading things to a witness and asking is this what is written in the document, I don't think we're getting to any reliable evidence that is of relevance to this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I haven't asked the witness to confirm if -- if I've read a section accurately. I've asked the witness if, according to his knowledge of events in Sanski Most, whether the actions described by Arkan in this article are a continuation of those events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your question was: "Sir, would you agree that, according to this report, Arkan and his men continued in Prijedor what they had started in Sanski Most?"

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that's according to this report. In fact, whether he agrees with that report or doesn't agree with the report, the report says so anyway. You're really not getting much mileage by asking that kind of question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would only add that the report doesn't say what Arkan had been doing in Sanski Most, and that's knowledge that the witness has. Although I won't insist on the question, but I would like to tender the document either through this particular witness or from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We would object through the witness, as the witness has not shown any knowledge to be able to authenticate the document or give any reliability to it. As for the bar table, I think we've stated multiple times before. Your Honours have issued a guidance when bar table submissions by the Prosecution were due. That time has long past, and the Prosecution still insists on amending its case and adding to its case with documents that were not presented during the original time-period but they've not shown due diligence why they did not seek them at that time and are now trying to adduce evidence positive for their case after their case is closed. And we believe that is not only a violation of Your Honours' guidance is also wholly improper, according to the rules of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Defence have submitted a statement from this witness with a paragraph that deals with Arkan's activities in Sanski Most in September 1995. This document -- this report is contemporaneous in respect to Arkan's activities, and it is the practice in this Trial Chamber that's been clarified a number of times, and I refer to the guidance we received on the 29th of October, 2012, that if the content of a document is sufficiently linked to the content of a witness's testimony, then it is admissible. And this document is very clearly relevant. It relates to forcible transfer of non-Serbs from Serb-claimed territory, and it is a part of our indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can MFI it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just add one additional thing: Mr. Jeremy has now conceded what I've been claiming all along, that these documents are part of their indictment.
